event.title: Creating the 'ugly shirt'
event.subtitle: Or how I misunderstood 'Zero History'
event.abstract: How I created the 'ugly shirt' from the book 'don't create the ugly shirt' (Zero History).
event.description: Some fun research based upon my misunderstanding of the ugly shirt as described by William Gibson in Zero History. Multiple iterations of 'an' ugly shirt already exist, as is the research into counter surveillance very wide, with both facial recognition disruption, counter illumination and so on. But what if we take this idea a bit further into the realm of 'global conspiracy'. Which would also be fitting for a Gibson novel.

event.title: Uxn
event.subtitle: small computing
event.description:
You might wonder how small you can go still have an interactive and self-hosted computing system, or what happens when you don't have an internet connection for months. Uxn is one attempt to answer these questions. It is a computing stack developed by Rek Bella and Devine Lu Linvega (collectively Hundred Rabbits), who travel around the world on their sailboat. I haven't sailed in about 20 years, but I find these solarpunk perspectives interesting.
Uxn is stack-based processor, usually implemented as an emulator running on whatever hardware is available. Uxntal is programming language, somewhere between Assembly and Forth. Varvara is the set of peripherals usually attached to an Uxn processor. I made my own, slightly different thing based on a Raspberry Pi Pico / RP2040.

event.title: UEFI: What's So Unified About It?
event.abstract: An introduction to how UEFI works and what it is that makes it "unified", how to discover things in areas you have no clue about through practice, and a case study of this via a bootloader I wrote from scratch with no prior domain-specific knowledge.

event.title: Modal logic for fun and non-profit
event.abstract: A talk explaining the basics of formal logic and describing various technical and non-technical applications. Focusing specifically on modal logic, because it's very useful and deserves more attention in my opinion!
event.description:
Formal logic is cool because it can be applied not just to technical topics like mathematics or programming, but really any topic where "reasoning" is involved. Typically, a basic course in logic will teach you about propositional logic as a basis, and then move on to predicate logic as a more powerful tool. But in between those two forms of logic exists a third in terms of expressivity: modal logic, which allows talking about the *ways* in which statements might be true or false. This makes modal logic useful to analyze individual programs or distributed systems, but also fun stuff like board game strategies. And because modal logic is still simpler than predicate logic, it is easier to work with and in many cases even allows for algorithmic checking - which also powers formal verification tools like TLA+ and Alloy.
This talk should be accessible for those without any background in formal logic - I will go over the basics before diving deeper into modal logic. All you'll need is some familiarity with programming and a willingness to look at weird maths symbols. :>
